## Welcome {#home}

### Radiation and Noise

**Learning Objectives:**

- Distinguish ionizing from non-ionizing radiation
- Identify natural and man-made sources of radiation exposure
- Describe radiation units and biological effects by dose
- Apply the principles of radiation protection, including ALARA
- Define noise, its properties, and its auditory and non-auditory effects
- Outline strategies for noise control

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
Final sub-chapter of the Environment section's four-part sequence
(Water → Air → Light → Radiation). Noise is included alongside
radiation since both are physical environmental hazards not covered
elsewhere in the curriculum, and the source material treats them
together.
:::

## Ionizing vs. Non-Ionizing Radiation {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Radiation** is energy emitted as electromagnetic waves or moving
subatomic particles.

| | Ionizing | Non-ionizing |
|---|---|---|
| **Examples** | X-rays, gamma rays (EM); alpha and beta particles (corpuscular) | UV, visible light, infrared, microwave, radio-frequency |
| **Mechanism** | Removes tightly-bound electrons, creating ions; penetrates and damages tissue | Generally causes heating effects only |
| **Danger** | Alpha particles: ~10× more harmful than X/gamma rays if internalized (inhaled/ingested), but poor external penetration; gamma/X-rays: short wavelength, deeply penetrating | Comparatively low energy, less harmful |

---

## Sources of Radiation Exposure {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

**Natural (~0.1 rad/year total):** cosmic rays (higher at altitude — a
commercial pilot receives ~300 mrad/year), terrestrial radiation from
radioactive elements in soil/rock (much higher in uranium-bearing
regions, e.g. parts of Kerala), and internal radiation from radioactive
material (K40, etc.) normally present in body tissue.

**Man-made:** **medical/dental X-rays are the largest man-made source**
of population radiation exposure; radioactive fallout from nuclear
explosions (Cs137, Sr90 — both persist for decades, half-lives of
~28–30 years); minor contributions from everyday items.

---

## Radiation Units {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

| Quantity | Older unit | SI unit |
|---|---|---|
| Activity (disintegrations/time) | Curie (Ci) | Becquerel (Bq) |
| Exposure (ionization in air) | Roentgen | Coulomb/kg |
| Absorbed dose (energy/mass) | Rad | Gray (Gy) — 1 rad = 0.01 Gy |
| Dose equivalent (biological effect) | Rem | Sievert (Sv) — 1 Sv = 100 rem |

**Dose equivalent (H) = Absorbed dose (D) × Quality factor (Q)** — Q = 1
for X-rays/gamma rays/electrons, but Q = 20 for alpha particles,
reflecting their much greater biological damage per unit of absorbed
energy.

---

## Biological Effects by Dose {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Acute whole-body exposure produces a dose-dependent spectrum:

| Dose (rad) | Effect |
|---|---|
| <5 | No observable effect |
| 5–150 | Detectable blood changes; nausea/fatigue at the higher end |
| 150–1,100 | Severe blood changes; at 300–500 rad, up to 50% mortality within 60 days without intensive care (bone marrow destruction) |
| 1,100–2,000 | Near-certain death within 1–2 weeks (GI system destruction) |
| >2,000 | Death is certain; >5,000 rad disables CNS control of breathing/circulation |

**Genetic effects** differ from somatic effects: somatic damage appears
within the exposed person's lifetime, while genetic effects (from
chromosome/point mutations) appear in offspring.

---

## Radiation Protection {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Permissible dose:** additional man-made exposure should not exceed
  **5 rad/year**, on top of ~0.1 rad/year natural background
- **Shielding:** lead aprons (0.5 mm lead) reduce scattered X-ray
  intensity by over 90% for occupationally exposed workers
- **Monitoring:** film badges/dosimeters track cumulative worker
  exposure
- **Governing bodies:** the International Commission on Radiological
  Protection (ICRP), IAEA, and WHO set and coordinate international dose
  limits and safety recommendations — this field is termed
  **radiation hygiene**

---

## ALARA: Time, Distance, and Shielding {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Radiation protection in practice is organized around three controllable
factors, together following the **ALARA principle** ("As Low As
Reasonably Achievable") — exposure should always be minimized, even
when it is below the permissible dose limit:

- **Time** — minimize time spent near a radiation source; exposure is
  directly proportional to duration
- **Distance** — exposure falls off with the **inverse square of
  distance**, so even a small increase in distance from the source
  substantially reduces dose
- **Shielding** — material (e.g. the lead aprons already mentioned)
  placed between the source and the person absorbs radiation before it
  reaches them

**Why ALARA matters as a principle, not just a limit:** the 5 rad/year
permissible dose is a ceiling, not a target — ALARA pushes practice to
minimize exposure well below that ceiling whenever reasonably possible,
the same logic used elsewhere in this course for "no safe threshold"
exposures.

---

## Noise: Definition and Sources {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Noise** is best defined as *"wrong sound, in the wrong place, at the
wrong time"* — not simply "unwanted sound," since that definition is
too subjective. The term **"noise pollution"** captures its status as a
modern public-health hazard.

**Sources:** automobiles, aircraft, industry (acute near railway
junctions, traffic circles, airports); domestic sources (TV, radio); and
recreational sources (loudspeakers, pressure horns).

**Properties:**

- **Loudness** — measured in **decibels (dB)**; normal conversation
  60–65 dB, whispering 20–30 dB, boiler factories ~120 dB. Daily exposure
  up to **85 dB** is broadly the tolerable limit for hearing
- **Frequency** — measured in **Hertz (Hz)**; the human ear detects
  roughly 20–20,000 Hz

---

## Effects of Noise Exposure {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Auditory:** noise-induced hearing loss, classically showing a
  characteristic dip at **4,000 Hz** on audiogram
- **Non-auditory:**
  - Interference with speech communication (300–500 Hz range most
    disruptive)
  - Annoyance (a psychological response, more pronounced in neurotic
    individuals)
  - Reduced work efficiency and concentration
  - Physiological changes — raised blood pressure, raised intracranial
    pressure, increased heart/breathing rate, sweating, sleep
    interference

---

## Control of Noise {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

- **Urban planning** — zoning to separate industrial/transport areas
  from residential; green belts between roads and housing
- **Vehicle control** — restricting heavy vehicles on narrow/residential
  streets; prohibiting indiscriminate horn use
- **Building design** — acoustic insulation, detached rather than
  continuous construction
- **Occupational protection** — hearing protection mandatory above
  85 dB, worker rotation away from noisy areas, periodic audiometry
- **Legislation and education** — legal noise limits plus public
  awareness, since no noise-abatement programme succeeds without
  community participation

- No relationship to distance
